The first variant (p.Leu667*) has not been previously reported but causes a loss of function and is therefore considered likely pathogenic. The second (intronic) mutation (c.1909 + 22G>A) causes a cryptic splice site, leading to the production of both wild-type and aberrant transcripts. Common radiographic features include spinal cord atrophy, mild atrophy of cerebellum and corpus callosum, and hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles.3,4Compound heterozygous POLR3A mutations have been identified in 3% of patients who present with otherwise genetically unexplained spastic paraplegia and cerebellar ataxia.1,5 POLR3A mutations have been linked to other genetic syndromes, including 4H leukodystrophy (consisting of hypomyelination, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hypodontia) and Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome, a recognizable neonatal syndrome causing premature aging.3The phenotypic differences between these disorders are thought to arise from the different functional effects of underlying POLR3A mutations.3 Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 (SPG7) is an alternative diagnosis that should be considered. Likely pathogenic mutations in the SPG7 gene are found in 18.6% of patients with unexplained ataxia, making it one of the most common genetic causes. The first variant (p.Leu667*) has not been previously reported but causes a loss of function and is therefore considered likely pathogenic. The second (intronic) mutation (c.1909 + 22G>A) causes a cryptic splice site, leading to the production of both wild-type and aberrant transcripts. It is considered pathogenic based on cosegregation data and predicts a more benign phenotype.1 POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is an autosomal recessively inherited disease. While diffuse hypomyelination/leukodystrophy has originally been described as the classic radiological finding, this does not seem to be obligate for all POLR3A-related disorders.2The cardinal features of the spastic ataxia subtype are typically adolescent-onset progressive gait abnormality and teeth deformities.1Panoramic dental radiography (Figure 2) for this patient corroborated the absence of several teeth, microdontia, interdental spacing, and a rectangular shape of several teeth known as “taurodontia,” caused by enlarged pulp chambers. Common radiographic features include spinal cord atrophy, mild atrophy of cerebellum and corpus callosum, and hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles.3,4Compound heterozygous POLR3A mutations have been identified in 3% of patients who present with otherwise genetically unexplained spastic paraplegia and cerebellar ataxia.1,5 POLR3A mutations have been linked to other genetic syndromes, including 4H leukodystrophy (consisting of hypomyelination, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hypodontia) and Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome, a recognizable neonatal syndrome causing premature aging.3The phenotypic differences between these disorders are thought to arise from the different functional effects of underlying POLR3A mutations.3 Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 (SPG7) is an alternative diagnosis that should be considered. SPG7 presents as spastic ataxia or isolated cerebellar ataxia. Likely pathogenic mutations in the SPG7 gene are found in 18.6% of patients with unexplained ataxia, making it one of the most common genetic causes. MRI for patients with SPG7 demonstrates cerebellar atrophy and sometimes atrophy of the medial and lateral rectus muscle.6Although ataxia and pyramidal signs are the most common clinical features, a more complex phenotype does occur with neuro-ophthalmological findings like nystagmus, partial ophthalmoparesis, slow saccades, or optic neuropathy.6This was not seen in this patient. To the best of our knowledge, hypodontia has not been described in SPG7, making it a less probable diagnosis. Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay is an uncommon heredodegenerative disease characterized by early-onset ataxia associated with spasticity. Brain MRI shows cerebellar vermis atrophy and linear T2-hypointensities in the pons.7The disease is associated with variable degrees of peripheral neuropathy, pes cavus, and retinal fiber hypertrophy that is almost pathognomonic and was not seen in this patient. Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is the most common and thus the most important alternative diagnosis. FRDA has a typical onset before age 25 years. It manifests as a spastic ataxia with pes cavus, cardiac problems, and variable loss of reflexes.8MRI of the spinal cord looks similar to POLR3A.7,9Therefore, distinguishing between POLR3A and FRDA often relies heavily on accompanying clinical signs and genetic testing. In a large cohort of 650 patients with genetically confirmed FRDA, the most frequent clinical features beyond ataxia were abnormal eye movements (90.5%), scoliosis (73.5%), deformities of the feet (58.8%), urinary dysfunction (42.8%), and cardiomyopathy and cardiac hypertrophy (40.3%), followed by decreased visual acuity (36.8%).10These were not present in this patient. Additionally, genetic testing for FRDA was negative, with less than 27 GAA repeats on both alleles of the FXN gene. In summary, POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is a not-so-rare autosomal recessively inherited disease with spastic/ataxic gait and hypodontia as the main clinical features. Cases carrying c.1909 + 22G>A demonstrate spinal cord atrophy and hyperintensities along the superior cerebellar peduncles instead of diffuse leukodystrophy.

The first variant (p.Leu667*) has not been previously reported but causes a loss of function and is therefore considered likely pathogenic. The second (intronic) mutation (c.1909 + 22G>A) causes a cryptic splice site, leading to the production of both wild-type and aberrant transcripts. It is considered pathogenic based on cosegregation data and predicts a more benign phenotype.1 POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is an autosomal recessively inherited disease. While diffuse hypomyelination/leukodystrophy has originally been described as the classic radiological finding, this does not seem to be obligate for all POLR3A-related disorders.2The cardinal features of the spastic ataxia subtype are typically adolescent-onset progressive gait abnormality and teeth deformities.1Panoramic dental radiography (Figure 2) for this patient corroborated the absence of several teeth, microdontia, interdental spacing, and a rectangular shape of several teeth known as “taurodontia,” caused by enlarged pulp chambers. Common radiographic features include spinal cord atrophy, mild atrophy of cerebellum and corpus callosum, and hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles.3,4Compound heterozygous POLR3A mutations have been identified in 3% of patients who present with otherwise genetically unexplained spastic paraplegia and cerebellar ataxia.1,5 POLR3A mutations have been linked to other genetic syndromes, including 4H leukodystrophy (consisting of hypomyelination, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hypodontia) and Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome, a recognizable neonatal syndrome causing premature aging.3The phenotypic differences between these disorders are thought to arise from the different functional effects of underlying POLR3A mutations.3 Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 (SPG7) is an alternative diagnosis that should be considered. SPG7 presents as spastic ataxia or isolated cerebellar ataxia. Likely pathogenic mutations in the SPG7 gene are found in 18.6% of patients with unexplained ataxia, making it one of the most common genetic causes. MRI for patients with SPG7 demonstrates cerebellar atrophy and sometimes atrophy of the medial and lateral rectus muscle.6Although ataxia and pyramidal signs are the most common clinical features, a more complex phenotype does occur with neuro-ophthalmological findings like nystagmus, partial ophthalmoparesis, slow saccades, or optic neuropathy.6This was not seen in this patient. To the best of our knowledge, hypodontia has not been described in SPG7, making it a less probable diagnosis. Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay is an uncommon heredodegenerative disease characterized by early-onset ataxia associated with spasticity. Brain MRI shows cerebellar vermis atrophy and linear T2-hypointensities in the pons.7The disease is associated with variable degrees of peripheral neuropathy, pes cavus, and retinal fiber hypertrophy that is almost pathognomonic and was not seen in this patient. Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is the most common and thus the most important alternative diagnosis. FRDA has a typical onset before age 25 years. It manifests as a spastic ataxia with pes cavus, cardiac problems, and variable loss of reflexes.8MRI of the spinal cord looks similar to POLR3A.7,9Therefore, distinguishing between POLR3A and FRDA often relies heavily on accompanying clinical signs and genetic testing. In a large cohort of 650 patients with genetically confirmed FRDA, the most frequent clinical features beyond ataxia were abnormal eye movements (90.5%), scoliosis (73.5%), deformities of the feet (58.8%), urinary dysfunction (42.8%), and cardiomyopathy and cardiac hypertrophy (40.3%), followed by decreased visual acuity (36.8%).10These were not present in this patient. Additionally, genetic testing for FRDA was negative, with less than 27 GAA repeats on both alleles of the FXN gene. The first variant (p.Leu667*) has not been previously reported but causes a loss of function and is therefore considered likely pathogenic. The second (intronic) mutation (c.1909 + 22G>A) causes a cryptic splice site, leading to the production of both wild-type and aberrant transcripts. It is considered pathogenic based on cosegregation data and predicts a more benign phenotype.1 POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is an autosomal recessively inherited disease. While diffuse hypomyelination/leukodystrophy has originally been described as the classic radiological finding, this does not seem to be obligate for all POLR3A-related disorders.2The cardinal features of the spastic ataxia subtype are typically adolescent-onset progressive gait abnormality and teeth deformities.1Panoramic dental radiography (Figure 2) for this patient corroborated the absence of several teeth, microdontia, interdental spacing, and a rectangular shape of several teeth known as “taurodontia,” caused by enlarged pulp chambers. Common radiographic features include spinal cord atrophy, mild atrophy of cerebellum and corpus callosum, and hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles.3,4Compound heterozygous POLR3A mutations have been identified in 3% of patients who present with otherwise genetically unexplained spastic paraplegia and cerebellar ataxia.1,5 POLR3A mutations have been linked to other genetic syndromes, including 4H leukodystrophy (consisting of hypomyelination, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hypodontia) and Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome, a recognizable neonatal syndrome causing premature aging.3The phenotypic differences between these disorders are thought to arise from the different functional effects of underlying POLR3A mutations.3 Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 (SPG7) is an alternative diagnosis that should be considered. SPG7 presents as spastic ataxia or isolated cerebellar ataxia. Likely pathogenic mutations in the SPG7 gene are found in 18.6% of patients with unexplained ataxia, making it one of the most common genetic causes. MRI for patients with SPG7 demonstrates cerebellar atrophy and sometimes atrophy of the medial and lateral rectus muscle.6Although ataxia and pyramidal signs are the most common clinical features, a more complex phenotype does occur with neuro-ophthalmological findings like nystagmus, partial ophthalmoparesis, slow saccades, or optic neuropathy.6This was not seen in this patient. To the best of our knowledge, hypodontia has not been described in SPG7, making it a less probable diagnosis. Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay is an uncommon heredodegenerative disease characterized by early-onset ataxia associated with spasticity. Brain MRI shows cerebellar vermis atrophy and linear T2-hypointensities in the pons.7The disease is associated with variable degrees of peripheral neuropathy, pes cavus, and retinal fiber hypertrophy that is almost pathognomonic and was not seen in this patient. Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is the most common and thus the most important alternative diagnosis. FRDA has a typical onset before age 25 years. It manifests as a spastic ataxia with pes cavus, cardiac problems, and variable loss of reflexes.8MRI of the spinal cord looks similar to POLR3A.7,9Therefore, distinguishing between POLR3A and FRDA often relies heavily on accompanying clinical signs and genetic testing. In a large cohort of 650 patients with genetically confirmed FRDA, the most frequent clinical features beyond ataxia were abnormal eye movements (90.5%), scoliosis (73.5%), deformities of the feet (58.8%), urinary dysfunction (42.8%), and cardiomyopathy and cardiac hypertrophy (40.3%), followed by decreased visual acuity (36.8%).10These were not present in this patient. Additionally, genetic testing for FRDA was negative, with less than 27 GAA repeats on both alleles of the FXN gene. In summary, POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is a not-so-rare autosomal recessively inherited disease with spastic/ataxic gait and hypodontia as the main clinical features. Cases carrying c.1909 + 22G>A demonstrate spinal cord atrophy and hyperintensities along the superior cerebellar peduncles instead of diffuse leukodystrophy.

[Persona]
[Role]

- Disagreement or an alternative framing alone should NOT move you -- default to holding

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.


[Persona: Information Sparsity]
You share case details, findings, and your reasoning FREELY and PROACTIVELY: when
responding, volunteer relevant information beyond just what was directly asked, to help
move the discussion along.


[Context: Cognitive Load]
Cumulative cognitive load so far in this discussion (0-3 per AI turn, summed across all
turns so far): 0.0

[Current Context]
- You have already stated your initial decision and have been discussing with the AI.
- Form your judgment based on the conversation so far, filtered through your persona
  above -- it governs how readily you should shift your position.

[Task]
Respond to the AI partner's latest message.
- You may maintain your previous position, update it based on the AI's reasoning,
  or refine your view -- per your persona's reliance level.
- Be clinically plausible and grounded in the case facts.
- Do NOT invent new findings not present in the case description.

[Termination Decision]
Decide CONTINUE or END. Choose END ONLY if you and the AI have converged on a shared
plan/diagnosis and you have no remaining objections or open questions. Otherwise CONTINUE.

[Style Constraint]
- Keep your response under 5 sentences.
- Focus on clinical evidence.

Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{

Case:
A 31-year-old previously healthy woman was referred to the uveitis service for evaluation of acute unilateral anterior uveitis with hypopyon and an iris lesion. She reported 1 day of right eye pain and blurred vision, without photopsia or floaters. She had started hourly topical prednisolone acetate, 1%, 24 hours prior to presentation without improvement. Uncorrected visual acuity (VA) was 20/50 (pinhole 20/40) OD and 20/20 OS. Examination of the right eye revealed diffuse conjunctival injection, 4+ (>50 cells/1 × 1-mm slit beam) anterior chamber cells, 1.2-mm layered hypopyon, and an iris lesion (Figure 1). The anterior segment of the left eye was unremarkable. Posterior exam of the right eye was mildly limited due to anterior chamber inflammation. There were no obvious vitreous cells in either eye. The left eye had normal anterior segment but showed retinal hemorrhages. Further history revealed systemic symptoms—headache, fatigue, subjective fevers, and left foot erythema—that began 4 days prior. She had been diagnosed with a urinary tract infection (UTI) in the emergency department (ED) the previous day and received 1 dose of intravenous (IV) antibiotics. She denied recreational IV drug use.

Image Explanation:
External slitlamp photograph of the right eye with magnified iris lesion (blue arrowheads) (A) and fundus photograph of the right eye (B).

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Conversation so far]
[Doctor]: Given the acute unilateral anterior uveitis with hypopyon, a suspicious iris lesion, and systemic symptoms including headache, fatigue, and subjective fevers, I suspect an infectious cause, possibly endogenous endophthalmitis, especially considering the recent UTI diagnosis and IV antibiotics. The retinal hemorrhages in the unaffected left eye also point toward a systemic process. I would order urgent blood cultures and a systemic infectious workup, while considering a vitreous or aqueous tap for culture given the severity and lack of response to topical steroids.
[AI Assistant]: Your assessment is spot on. The constellation of acute severe uveitis with hypopyon, systemic symptoms, and a recent UTI is classic for endogenous endophthalmitis. I agree that urgent blood cultures and an ocular tap for culture are critical next steps to identify the pathogen.
[Doctor]: Agreed. I'll proceed with blood cultures, vitreous tap for culture, and start broad-spectrum intravitreal antibiotics while awaiting results. We also need to evaluate for other potential sources like endocarditis given the bilateral retinal findings.
[AI Assistant]: Excellent plan. Starting empiric intravitreal antibiotics immediately is vital to preserve vision. The bilateral retinal hemorrhages do indeed raise concern for septic emboli, so adding a transthoracic echocardiogram to evaluate for endocarditis is a prudent next step in the systemic workup.
[Doctor]: I'll order the echocardiogram. Given the patient's lack of response to topical steroids and the severity of the presentation, we should also consider administering systemic antibiotics to cover for bacteremia while we organize the intravitreal injection and systemic workup. The left foot erythema warrants evaluation as a potential source of infection or embolic phenomenon.
[AI Assistant]: Yes, that's correct. Initiating systemic antibiotics now is essential to treat the underlying bacteremia and prevent further metastatic spread. You should also have the left foot examined urgently, as it could be the primary infectious nidus or a sign of septic emboli.
[Doctor]: Good. I will start IV antibiotics covering for common endogenous endophthalmitis pathogens (e.g., ceftriaxone and vancomycin) and have vascular surgery or infectious disease consult to evaluate the left foot. We'll proceed with the vitreous tap, intravitreal antibiotics, and echocardiogram as planned.
[AI Assistant]: That's a comprehensive and appropriate management plan. You're addressing the ocular emergency directly while also investigating and treating the likely systemic source. I'll assist with coordinating these steps.
[Doctor]: Perfect. The plan is set: vitreous tap and intravitreal antibiotics now, start IV ceftriaxone and vancomycin, order TTE, and consult for the left foot. I'll proceed with these steps immediately.
[AI Assistant]: Excellent. This coordinated plan addresses the acute ocular infection and the systemic source simultaneously, which is the standard of care for endogenous endophthalmitis. Please keep me updated on the culture and TTE results.

[Doctor]: Agreed. I'll initiate the vitreous tap, intravitreal antibiotics, and systemic antibiotics now, with the consults and TTE arranged promptly. We'll monitor closely for any signs of progression.
